items.title: England leave Jones sucking lemons but demolition of Japan shows widening gulf | Gerard Meagher
items.desc:
Brave Blossoms looked like Sunday afternoon amateurs but the one-sided result highlights the failings of the international landscape

What can we surmise from that? England are very good at shooting fish in a barrel. Max Ojomoh looks the part when given the freedom of Twickenham in which to operate. Will Joseph can finish, Maro Itoje can remove candy from the clutches of a baby and someone on the TV production crew has a sadistic streak.

After almost every England try – and there were 13 of them here – the camera would pan to Eddie Jones in the coaches’ box. His face that little more forlorn every time. One more lemon sucked. Japan had a man sent off before they had touched the ball and things got no better for the Brave Blossoms.

items.title: Five-try Will Joseph equals record as England steamroller Japan
items.desc:
• England 78-15 Japan

  • Steve Borthwick’s men score 13 tries

Not every game of rugby can deliver a result for the ages and this one never stood a chance of eclipsing the weekend’s remarkable events in Cardiff and Paris. In terms of one-sided contests at Twickenham down the years there have been few to match it although Will Joseph, England’s athletic new wing, will remember every detail for the rest of his days.

Joseph, playing only his second Test, ended up claiming a record-equalling five tries as his side comfortably topped their previous highest tally against the Brave Blossoms. From the moment he helped himself to a hat-trick of tries inside the game’s opening 20 minutes it was simply a question of how many points England would score and Maro Itoje’s side duly took advantage of the free buffet.

items.title: Wales’ Dewi Lake calls historic win against New Zealand ‘amazing feeling’
items.desc:
• ‘It’s nothing this group doesn’t deserve for their work’

  • Beauden Barrett: ‘Their defence felt like a brick wall’

Dewi Lake, the first Wales captain to lead his team to victory over New Zealand in 73 years, paid tribute to his teammates, who chiselled this win out of a recent history of adversity, sometimes even humiliation. At last, they gave this rugby nation reason to be proud again, as he called the win an “amazing feeling”.

“It’s nice to sit in this room and not be disappointed,” he said. “I think we got asked a lot of questions last week in terms of performance, in terms of things that went wrong. We had tough conversations in the week [after a narrow win over Japan]. We’re a group that trusts each other a lot, and to put on the field what we did today, to make history, it’s tough to put it into words really. But it is nothing this group doesn’t deserve for the work they put in for the last year, year and a half.”

items.title: Wales bury 73-year All Blacks hoodoo with seismic victory over New Zealand
items.desc:
• Wales 35-28 New Zealand

  • Home side secure first win over All Blacks since 1953

Just when you expect it the least. By what wild logic did Wales choose now to pull off a victory 73 years in the seeking? There may have been only 55,000 in Cardiff’s great stadium for this first win over New Zealand since 1953, but judging by the noise alone, Wales are back. They had managed five wins in 31 Tests since the last World Cup, all of them against teams outside the top eight, and they choose now to beat the All Blacks.

An extraordinary defensive display for the last half-hour kept wave after wave of New Zealand attacks at bay, each feat of heroism greeted as if the most sublime of tries by JPR, Gareth, Shane or JJ. None of those ever tasted this, but now a new generation of Welshmen, still young and hopeful, can add a win over the All Blacks to their CV.

• Interested clubs have until 1 February to come forward

Prem Rugby has fired the starting gun on expanding to 12 teams by formally asking interested clubs to come forward by February. The chief executive, Simon Massie-Taylor, is in the United States attempting to woo investors, with the Prem determined to add two more teams to its ranks for the 2029-30 competition.

Born in Plymouth, Devon, in 1993, Henry Slade is a centre for Exeter Chiefs and England. items.title: England braced for All Black-lash in the ultimate test of their mini-upturn
items.desc:
New Zealand should provide a huge reaction to their shock defeat in Wales with enticing clash even more instructive

From the Bay of Islands on the northern tip of New Zealand to Invercargill in the deep south, there is rare unanimity this week. Back in the day there would be parochial arguments about, say, the ratio of Aucklanders to Cantabrians in the starting XV. This time there is nationwide recognition that absolutely nothing matters beyond a bounce-back win for the boys in black on Saturday.

It is the inevitable upshot of last weekend’s seismic defeat by Wales, a result that prompted Dave Rennie, the head coach, to admit his reshuffled team had “let ourselves and our country down”. The former All Black scrum-half Justin Marshall went a step further. “We were arrogant enough to think that we could make those changes and still protect our history, and now look what’s happened,” a wounded Marshall told the GBRNRZ podcast.

items.title: Wales’ epic upset against All Blacks offers fresh hope for rank outsiders | Robert Kitson
items.desc:
The plot twist in Cardiff that nobody saw coming suggests the northern hemisphere is remobilising in time for next year’s World Cup

What does it take to beat the All Blacks in Cardiff? “I’ll never forget the pressure they put us under. I don’t think we were a better team than New Zealand, but there was a certain spirit in the Welsh side which pulled us through.” The vivid recollections of the late, great Cliff Morgan on Wales’s famous victory in 1953 could just as easily have applied to the long-awaited modern-day sequel on Saturday.

Seventy-three years. The last time it came to pass was the year Sir Edmund Hillary and Tenzing Norgay officially became the first people to conquer Everest. Some bookmakers had even stopped taking bets on an All Blacks win; in the buildup the Wales side were likened in one New Zealand newspaper to “Dickensian orphans” begging for scraps. More bread of heaven, please sir? Here was a plot twist nobody saw coming.

items.title: The Guardian view on sporting triumphs: more than just a game | Editorial
items.desc:
From Welsh rugby to English football, victories on the pitch can capture a nation’s imagination and briefly make the impossible seem possible

The world divides roughly in two: people who like sport and people who don’t see the point. George Orwell was roundly dismissive – “war minus the shooting”. Adrian Conan Doyle (Sir Arthur’s son) had the super-rationalist Sherlock Holmes baffled by why anyone should care that one horse could outrun another. Yet sport can do something that life rarely does: offer a comprehensible narrative, with a beginning, a middle and, gloriously, an end. Life is convoluted, messy and ultimately hard to assess; sport can offer resolution in 80 or 90 minutes. All of which is a long-winded way of saying: weren’t Wales magnificent in beating the All Blacks on Saturday?

Even those who don’t understand the finer points of the rolling maul can surely grasp why this result matters. For much of the last century, heavy industry and rugby were twin pillars of Welsh national identity. The heavy industry is largely gone, and over the past few years, rugby has looked to be going the same way: a weakened national team; financial problems that threatened to tear apart the domestic rugby set-up in Wales; and the growing appeal of football. Until Saturday, Welsh sports fans looking for a winning finish were better off watching the darts champion Gerwyn “The Iceman” Price than Steve Tandy’s rugby team.

items.title: England and New Zealand collide with final spots and reputations on the line
items.desc:
Discipline, bench impact and the breakdown will be pivotal in what home captain Maro Itoje says is a ‘massive game’

In the brave new world of the Nations Championship things are not as black and white as they used to be. Of course, England against New Zealand still has its own unique rattle and hum but the context is now slightly different. The winners of the Hillary Shield will have to wait a few hours until Ireland have faced South Africa and France have played Argentina to find out precisely where they stand.

Should the All Blacks triumph with a try bonus point they will be into next Sunday’s grand final regardless of how South Africa fare in Dublin. An England victory, on the other hand, would boost the Springboks and potentially set up a second successive showdown with New Zealand within eight days.

items.title: Expect a fearsome backlash from cornered All Blacks – but England must play with freedom | Ugo Monye
items.desc:
New Zealand want to ease the pain of defeat by Wales but England’s squad depth will make them formidable opponents

I’ve heard it said that in New Zealand, 65% of people are rugby fans but 95% are All Blacks fans. Regardless of how accurate those numbers are, the sentiment is clear, and it explains why Dave Rennie said his players had “let the country down” by losing to Wales. A backlash is coming at Twickenham.

I spent some time with Kieran Read this week, one of the greatest All Blacks to play the game. He enjoyed some fine wins over England during his career but also suffered two defeats and clearly still carries those scars. The pain and anguish remain and, after last weekend’s chastening defeat in Cardiff, the All Blacks will be burning.

• Itoje calls for players and fans to respect referees

Maro Itoje has said he will never adopt a win-at-all-costs mentality as England captain as he prepares to lead his side against the All Blacks at Twickenham on Saturday after a week in sport dominated by Rassie Erasmus’s “match-fixing” rant and sandpapergate.

Itoje has called on his “very good” side to take the next step towards greatness by clinching back-to-back victories over the All Blacks for the first time since 2003 but, guided by his Christian faith and moral compass, he is adamant there are lines he will not cross.

items.title: Rotated Wales aim to turn New Zealand miracle into true momentum against Australia
items.desc:
Steve Tandy has made four changes to his team to face wounded Wallabies after heroics against All Blacks

They beat the All Blacks for the first time in 73 years and they make four changes. The Wales coaching team could barely have shrugged their shoulders with any more nonchalance after what the rest of us thought was a pretty spectacular achievement last weekend if they had picked their under-20s for Saturday night’s follow-up against Australia in Cardiff. But, no, they are actually adding depth as well as quality to this new generation tasked with keeping the creaking structures of Welsh rugby upright for the foreseeable.

If anything, the changes make the team stronger. No matter they are without Adam Beard (shoulder injury but hopefully back for the finals next weekend), they see fit to drop/rest/let-attend-birth-of-first-child three other players too, including the player of the match last weekend.

items.title: The Breakdown | Rattled All Blacks face rare twin threat as England eye back-to-back scalps
items.desc:
After their seismic defeat by Wales, New Zealand face the prospect of history repeating itself in unwanted ways

They still talk about the last – and only – time the All Blacks contrived to lose twice in succession to England. Back in 2002-03, as now, there was a Rugby World Cup looming in Australia and New Zealand had no shortage of quality players. “There is so much talent in New Zealand that, if they don’t win the World Cup, there should be an inquiry,” opined Steve Hansen, Wales’s head coach at the time, before England’s fateful visit to Wellington in the summer of 2003.

There’s a fresh inquiry under way now, even before the All Blacks trot out of the Twickenham tunnel this Saturday for the 48th meeting between the two nations. While Saturday’s 35-28 defeat ended a 73-year wait for a Wales win, from a home perspective it has inevitably precipitated plenty of dark muttering back in the land of the long flat white.
